h1: Service charge, tips and staff incentives in an Indian brewpub
title: Service Charge and Tips in a Brewpub | Craft Beer School
desc: How Indian brewpubs can handle service charge, tips and staff incentives: the consumer guidelines, fair tip sharing and incentives that do not push drinking.
teaser: Service charge used to be a line on every bill. Now it is a question every brewpub owner has to answer properly.
standfirst: Tips and incentives shape how your floor team behaves. The rules on service charge have also shifted. Here is how to set up a fair, transparent system that keeps good staff and stays on the right side of consumer law.
sections:
For years many Indian restaurants and brewpubs added a service charge to every bill. In 2022 the Central Consumer Protection Authority issued guidelines saying a service charge cannot be added automatically or by default, cannot be collected under another name and must be left to the customer's choice. The matter has since been argued in court. The position may continue to develop.

We are brewers, not lawyers. Check the current position with your lawyer or restaurant association before you print a menu. The practical effect for most owners is that service charge can no longer be treated as guaranteed income for the floor team.

In many brewpubs, service charge was quietly part of take-home pay. Remove or reduce it and some of your best servers start looking at the place next door. If service charge becomes optional, your pay structure has to stand on its own.

That means looking at base salary, meals, shift allowances and the way tips are shared as one package. Our guide to brewery staffing covers roles and hiring. This piece covers the money that moves around on the floor.

Tips paid voluntarily by customers belong, in spirit, to the team that served them. The question is how to divide them. Common approaches:

  • A pooled system where all tips go into one pot and are shared by points. Servers, bartenders, runners and kitchen staff each get a set number of points per shift.
  • Individual tips kept by the server, which rewards strong servers but leaves out the kitchen and the back bar.
  • A hybrid where a fixed share of each server's tips goes to the pool.

Whatever you choose, write it down, show staff the monthly figures and never let management dip into the pool. Nothing destroys trust faster than tips that vanish. Ask your accountant how tips and incentives should be treated for payroll and tax, because the answer affects how you record them.

The people who make the beer rarely see a tip. They work early shifts, lift heavy kegs and clean hot vessels, then watch the floor share the evening's tips. Including the brewing team in the pool by a small share, or in a quarterly bonus tied to quality and consistency, says their work counts. It also helps with something we see too often in this trade, which is brewers burning out and leaving.
Incentives that do not push drinking

Incentives shape behaviour, so choose what you reward carefully. Paying staff a cut of every extra pint sold encourages them to push rounds on guests who have had enough. That is bad for guests, bad for your licence and bad for the brewpub's name.

Reward things that raise the quality of the visit instead:

  • Flights sold, since they introduce guests to more of your beer in smaller pours.
  • Food attached to beer orders.
  • Growler or can sales to take home, where your licence allows takeaway.
  • Good feedback scores and repeat bookings by name.

A useful floor rule: incentives are paid on average spend per cover, not litres per head. A table of four that shares a pairing platter and a flight each is worth more to you (and safer) than a table that orders a fourth round.
Making it work on the numbers

Every rupee of incentive is a cost, so it belongs in your monthly taproom economics. Set a budget for incentives as a share of revenue, track it monthly and adjust once a quarter rather than every week. Staff need to trust that the scheme will not change under their feet.

Explain the scheme at induction, in the language your team is most comfortable with. Put a one page summary on the staff noticeboard. When staff can work out their own monthly payout from the figures you share, arguments drop and the good servers stop wondering whether the grass is greener elsewhere.

Get the structure right and you hold on to the servers who know your beers, which is worth more than any single month's margin.
faqs: Can an Indian brewpub add a service charge to the bill?

Guidelines issued in 2022 say a service charge cannot be added by default and must be voluntary. The issue has been through the courts since. Check the current position with a lawyer before you set your billing.
What is a fair way to split tips?
Many brewpubs pool tips and share them by points per role and shift. Whatever you pick, write it down, share the figures with staff and keep management out of the pool.
Should staff be paid a commission on beer sold?
Avoid per-pint commissions, which encourage overserving. Reward flights, food pairings, takeaway sales and good feedback instead.
